Package frc.robot.subsystems.arm

Class SimArmSubsystem

java.lang.Object
edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.arm.AbstractArmSubsystem
frc.robot.subsystems.arm.SimArmSubsystem
All Implemented Interfaces:
edu.wpi.first.util.sendable.Sendable, edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Subsystem, Subsystem, AutoCloseable
public class SimArmSubsystem extends AbstractArmSubsystem
The arm implementation used in simulation, test runs, and CI.

This is a sibling of ArmSubsystem, not a configuration of it. Both extend AbstractArmSubsystem and therefore share the entire public API and control loop, but each supplies its own mechanism: the real one drives a motor controller, this one advances a WPILib SingleJointedArmSim. Nothing in the shared layer knows the difference.

Why a separate class rather than an IO behind the same subsystem. A team reading ArmSubsystem should see only the code that runs on their robot; a robot should never ship a physics model. Splitting by class makes that structural instead of a convention, and it means the simulation can own state the real mechanism has no use for — the plant, its step, and its thread — without that leaking into the hardware path. 


 // Robot code picks one once at startup:
 AbstractArmSubsystem arm = RobotBase.isReal()
     ? new ArmSubsystem(...)
     : new SimArmSubsystem(ArmHardware.CONSTANTS);

Why it wraps WPILib's model. SingleJointedArmSim already models a DC motor, a gearbox, moment of inertia, and a gravity load, and it is the model every team's simulation is calibrated against. Reimplementing it would drift from real results and would have to be maintained. Following the physics simulation guide, the closed loop is a WPILib PIDController plus ArmFeedforward; only the plumbing between the library's units and WPILib's doubles lives here. The same computation is used by ArmSubsystem for real hardware, so simulated and real mechanisms behave alike.

The gravity term is genuine. SingleJointedArmSim takes the arm's length and mass and applies a real, angle-dependent gravity load, so a simulated arm sags if it is not held. That is why the feedforward matters and why the tests are meaningful.

Units. WPILib's arm model measures angles in radians with zero horizontal. This library speaks rotations with the same zero reference, so the conversion is a single factor of 2&pi; and no offset. A hardware implementation that zeroes on a hard stop would apply its own offset instead.

Two ways to run it

Real-time — the default constructor starts a daemon thread that steps the plant every 20 ms, so the arm moves by itself exactly as it would on a robot. This is what a full robot simulation wants.

Stepped — SimArmSubsystem(ArmConstants, boolean) with false leaves time frozen until step(double) is called. This is what tests want: two identical runs then produce bit-identical trajectories, with no wall clock involved, so a suite cannot become flaky.

  • Constructor Details

    • SimArmSubsystem

      public SimArmSubsystem(ArmConstants constants)
      Creates a simulated arm that advances itself in real time.

      Use this for a full robot simulation, where nothing else is stepping the loop.

      Parameters:
      constants - the physical description of the mechanism

    • SimArmSubsystem

      public SimArmSubsystem(ArmConstants constants, boolean realTime)
      Creates a simulated arm, choosing whether it advances itself.

      Passing false is what makes a test deterministic: the plant only moves when the test calls step(double).

      Parameters:
      constants - the physical description of the mechanism
      realTime - true to step in the background, false to step on demand

    • holdAngle

      protected void holdAngle(edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Angle angle)
      Description copied from class: AbstractArmSubsystem
      Drives the arm to hold angle.

      Called once per loop while the mechanism is enabled. Implementations close the loop however suits their hardware: a vendor motor controller's onboard position control, or a WPILib PIDController plus feedforward, as ArmSubsystem and SimArmSubsystem both do.

      angle is already clamped to the travel range, so implementations need not re-validate it.

      Specified by:
      holdAngle in class AbstractArmSubsystem
      Parameters:
      angle - the angle to hold, measured from the zero position

    • driveOpenLoop

      protected void driveOpenLoop(double velocityRotationsPerSecond)
      Description copied from class: AbstractArmSubsystem
      Drives the arm open-loop at a velocity.

      Not reached from any command in this API; it exists so a subclass can build a calibration routine — drive into the lower stop until AbstractArmSubsystem.isAtLowerLimit() trips, then AbstractArmSubsystem.zeroPosition() — without reaching around the abstraction for raw voltage.

      Specified by:
      driveOpenLoop in class AbstractArmSubsystem
      Parameters:
      velocityRotationsPerSecond - the velocity to drive at, positive raising the arm

    • releaseOutput

      protected void releaseOutput()
      Description copied from class: AbstractArmSubsystem
      Stops commanding the mechanism.

      Called while idle and on SubsystemBase.stop(). Whether the arm then holds or sags is the hardware's brake mode, not a decision this method makes.

      Specified by:
      releaseOutput in class AbstractArmSubsystem

    • step

      public void step(double dtSeconds)
      Advances the simulated arm by one robot loop.

      The plant only moves when this is called, which is what makes a stepping test reproducible. Call it after SubsystemBase.periodic(), so the mechanism responds to this loop's command rather than the previous one's.

      Parameters:
      dtSeconds - the timestep to integrate, in seconds

    • isReal

      public boolean isReal()
      Description copied from interface: Subsystem
      Returns whether this mechanism is driving real hardware.

      Callers use this to skip hardware-only work, and tests use it to skip assertions that only make sense against real motors. A simulated implementation returns false.

      Returns:
      true for real hardware, false for a simulated implementation
